title: Start here: the basics
intro: Before the modules, get the words straight. This page explains, in plain language, the terms you will hear every day as an FDE: what a model actually is, how Claude the app differs from the Anthropic API, what a harness and a context are, open versus closed models, networks and VPCs, and why data privacy and security matter so much. Skim it once now, and come back whenever a word in a lesson is unclear.

groups.title: How an AI system works, layer by layer
groups.intro: Six pictures, each showing what actually happens at one layer: what the model does with your text, how it was trained, what the harness around it does, how an agent loops, what observability watches, and finally how all of it comes together to automate a real process safely and cheaply. The rest of this page explains each word in detail.

diagrams.title: 1. What an LLM does with your text
diagrams.caption: An LLM writes one token at a time. Each new token is added to the text and the whole loop runs again until it decides to stop. Nothing is looked up in a database; every word is a prediction.

steps.label: Your text arrives
steps.note: Instructions, data and the question

steps.label: Split into tokens
steps.note: Words and word pieces, about 3/4 of a word each

steps.label: Tokens become numbers
steps.note: Each token turns into a long list of numbers

steps.label: Layers weigh the context
steps.note: Attention links each token to the ones that matter

steps.label: Score every next token
steps.note: A probability for each possible next piece

steps.label: Pick one and add it
steps.note: Temperature controls how adventurous the pick is

diagrams.title: 2. How a model is trained
diagrams.caption: The first two steps make a model that can continue text. The next three turn it into an assistant that follows instructions and refuses harmful requests. All of it happens once, at the AI lab, before you ever call the model.

steps.label: Collect a huge amount of text
steps.note: Public web, books, code, licensed data

steps.label: Pre-training
steps.note: Predict the next token billions of times; adjust weights

steps.label: Instruction tuning
steps.note: Learn from examples of good answers to requests

steps.label: Feedback training
steps.note: Prefer answers people or rules rate as better

steps.label: Safety testing
steps.note: Red-team for harmful, biased or false output

steps.label: Release
steps.note: Offered through an app and an API

diagrams.title: 3. What a harness does around the model
diagrams.caption: The model only reads text and writes text. The harness is everything else: it builds the context, decides which tools the model may use, runs them, and keeps the record. Claude Code, Codex and your own app code are all harnesses.

steps.label: Replies, or asks to use a tool
Adds the result to the context
Logs it and returns the answer

diagrams.title: 4. What an agent is: a model working in a loop
diagrams.caption: A plain call is one question and one answer. An agent repeats plan, act, check until the goal is met or it hits a limit, then hands over. Limits on steps, tools and spending keep it safe.

steps.label: Goal given
steps.note: For example: resolve this invoice exception

steps.label: Plan the next action
steps.note: The model decides what to do next

steps.label: Use a tool
steps.note: Read a record, search a policy, draft an email

steps.label: Look at the result
steps.note: Did it work? What is still missing?

steps.label: Done or stuck?
steps.note: Stop and hand over, or loop again within limits

diagrams.title: 5. What observability watches
diagrams.caption: Observability is how you know the system is still doing its job after launch. Every call is traced, quality is scored, problems raise alerts, and the fixes are tested before release.

steps.label: Trace every call
steps.note: Input, output, tools used, tokens, time, cost

steps.label: Score quality
steps.note: Evals on real cases; spot checks by people

steps.label: Watch dashboards and alerts
steps.note: Error rate, cost per item, slow responses

steps.label: Read the failures
steps.note: Group them by cause

steps.label: Fix and re-test
steps.note: Prompt, tool, data or rule; run evals before release

diagrams.title: 6. All together: automating one process
diagrams.caption: Example: supplier invoice exceptions. Plain code does every step that follows a rule, the model only does the steps that need judgment, a person approves before anything is final, and every step is traced. That split is what keeps it secure, fast and cheap.

steps.label: Writes the result to the ERP

diagrams.title: What makes that system secure, fast and maintainable
diagrams.caption: Check every design against these three columns before you build.

columns.title: Secure
items: Each tool gets only the access it needs
Personal data masked before the model sees it
A person approves anything that changes records
Every action written to an audit log
Text from documents is treated as data, never as instructions

columns.title: Fast and low cost
items: Plain code for every rule-based step
Smallest model that passes the evals for each step
Cache repeated instructions and documents
Batch work that does not need an instant answer
Timeouts and retries so one slow call does not block

columns.title: Maintainable
items: Model name, prompts and limits in config, not code
Evals run before every change goes live
Traces show exactly what happened
A runbook and a named owner
Builds on the client's existing systems

groups.title: AI, models and LLMs
groups.intro: Most confusion starts here. A model is not a database and not a search engine. It is a trained pattern machine that writes the most likely next piece of text. Once that clicks, a lot of its behavior, good and bad, makes sense.

diagrams.title: How a model comes to exist, and how you use it
diagrams.caption: The first three steps happen once, at the AI lab. You only do the last two, every time you send a request.

steps.label: Collect huge amounts of text
steps.note: Public web, books, code, licensed data

steps.label: Pre-training
steps.note: Learn to predict the next token; weeks on thousands of chips

steps.label: Post-training
steps.note: Teach it to follow instructions and be safe

steps.label: Your prompt goes in
steps.note: Instructions, data, question

steps.label: Inference
steps.note: Model writes the answer one token at a time

terms.one: Software that does tasks we used to think needed human judgment: reading, writing, recognizing images, making predictions.
terms.why: It is an umbrella word. When a client says AI, ask what they actually mean: a chatbot, a prediction, document reading or automation.

terms.one: Building software by letting it learn patterns from examples, instead of a person writing every rule.
terms.like: Showing a new clerk a thousand past invoices instead of handing them a rulebook for every supplier.
terms.why: Machine learning depends on data. The quality of the examples decides the quality of the result.

terms.one: The product of training: a very large set of numbers that turns an input into an output. It does not look answers up in a stored table; it computes a likely answer from patterns it learned.
terms.like: A well-read person's trained intuition, not a filing cabinet.
terms.why: Because a model computes rather than retrieves, it can sound fluent and still be wrong. When exact facts matter, give it the source text.
terms.vs: A database stores records and returns exactly what was saved. A model stores patterns and generates new text.

terms.one: The numbers inside a model that training adjusts. Model size is often quoted in billions of parameters, such as a 70B model.
terms.why: Bigger usually means more capable but slower and more expensive to run. It matters most when you host a model yourself.

terms.one: The large, one-time training run where the model reads a vast amount of text and learns to predict the next piece of it.
terms.why: This is done by AI labs at enormous cost. On a client project you use a trained model; you do not train one.

terms.one: Extra training after pre-training. Post-training turns a raw text predictor into a helpful assistant that follows instructions. Fine-tuning adapts a model to a narrow task with your own examples.
terms.why: Fine-tuning is rarely the first step. Good prompts and retrieval are cheaper, faster and easier to change.

terms.one: Using a trained model to produce an output. Every request you send is one inference.
terms.why: Inference is what you pay for, per use, and what decides how fast your solution responds.

terms.one: A model trained to predict the next piece of text from the text before it.
terms.like: The word suggestions on your phone keyboard, scaled up enormously.
terms.why: Answering questions, summarizing, translating and writing code all come from this one skill done extremely well.

terms.one: A language model with billions of parameters, trained on a very large amount of text and code. Examples: Claude (Anthropic), GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), Llama (Meta), and models from Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen.
terms.why: LLMs are general purpose. The same model can sort tickets, draft emails, read contracts and write SQL.

terms.one: The unit an LLM reads and writes: a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. A common rule of thumb for English is that 100 tokens is about 75 words.
terms.why: Prices, limits and speed are all measured in tokens, so you will estimate them in every business case.

terms.one: How an LLM writes: it predicts one token, adds it to the text, then predicts the next, until it decides to stop.
terms.why: There is no finished answer waiting inside. Clear instructions at the start shape every step that follows.

terms.one: A setting that controls how much randomness goes into choosing each next token. Lower is more repeatable; higher is more varied.
terms.why: The same prompt can give different answers. For extraction and classification keep randomness low, and still test the output.

terms.one: When a model states something false with confidence, such as an invented citation or a policy clause that does not exist.
terms.why: It follows directly from predicting likely text without checking facts. Ground answers in sources and measure them on real cases.

terms.one: Models that work through intermediate steps before giving the final answer. Claude, OpenAI and Gemini all offer this mode.
terms.why: Better on multi-step problems, but it uses more tokens and takes longer. Turn it on where it earns its cost.

terms.one: A model that accepts more than text: images, PDFs and sometimes audio.
terms.why: Many client documents are scans, photos and screenshots. Multimodal models can read them directly.

terms.one: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. Made by an embedding model.
terms.why: Embeddings let you search documents by meaning, not just keywords. That is the search step inside most RAG systems.

groups.title: Companies, apps, APIs and harnesses
groups.intro: One company can offer the same model in several ways: a chat app for people, an API for programs, and ready-made tools such as coding agents. They share a model but differ in price, data terms and what you can build. When a client says we use Claude or we use ChatGPT, your first question is: which one?

diagrams.title: Same models, three different products
diagrams.caption: The pattern is the same at every major provider. Pick the column that matches what you are building.

columns.title: Chat app
items: Claude app, ChatGPT, Gemini app
For people typing and reading
Paid per seat or subscription
Data terms depend on the plan
Great for thinking and drafting

columns.title: API
items: Anthropic (Claude) API, OpenAI API, Gemini API
For your own programs to call
Paid per token used
You build the harness around it
How you build client solutions

columns.title: Coding agent
items: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI
For software work in a code repository
A ready-made harness on top of a model
Reads files, edits, runs commands
Review what it does before you trust it

diagrams.title: Where each piece sits
diagrams.caption: Read top to bottom: what the user touches first, down to the model and the hardware that runs it.

layers.label: Your app or workflow
layers.note: The screen, script or automation the client uses

layers.label: Harness
layers.note: Builds the prompt, keeps history, runs tools, decides when to stop

layers.label: API and SDK
layers.note: The order window your code sends requests to

layers.label: Model
layers.note: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama and others

layers.label: Infrastructure
layers.note: Chips and data centers run by the provider or a cloud

terms.one: A company that trains and serves models. Anthropic makes Claude. OpenAI makes GPT and Codex. Google makes Gemini. Meta makes Llama. Mistral, DeepSeek and Alibaba (Qwen) also publish models.
terms.why: Each has its own prices, terms, regions and strengths. Clients often already have a contract with one, which can decide your choice.

terms.one: Providers release models in families and versions. Claude, for example, comes as Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, from most capable to fastest and cheapest. Old versions are retired over time.
terms.why: Pin the exact model name in your code so results do not change underneath you, and plan for upgrades.

terms.one: The name of Anthropic's family of models, and also of the Claude app (web, desktop and mobile) where people chat with those models.
terms.why: Because one word means two things, always clarify: the app people use, or the model called from a system through the API.

terms.one: A finished product for people: you type, it answers. Examples: the Claude app, ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot. Sold as individual, team and enterprise plans.
terms.why: Excellent for research, drafting and learning. It is not how you build an automated process that runs without a person typing.

terms.one: Application Programming Interface: an agreed way for one program to ask another for data or actions over the network.
terms.like: A restaurant's order window. You hand in an order in the agreed format and get your food back; you never go into the kitchen.
terms.why: Everything you build talks to a model, and to the client's systems, through APIs.

terms.one: The developer service for calling Claude models from your own code, paid per token, using an API key from the Claude Console. Claude models are also offered through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry.
terms.why: This is how a POC uses Claude inside a client process: your code sends the document and instructions, and gets structured results back.
terms.vs: The Claude app is a product for people chatting. The API is a service for programs. Same models, but different billing, different controls and often different data terms.

terms.one: Software Development Kit: a library that makes an API easy to call from a language such as Python or TypeScript. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all publish official SDKs.
terms.why: Use the official SDK. It handles details such as retries and request formats so you write less code.

terms.one: A secret string that identifies your account when you call an API.
terms.why: Anyone holding it can spend your money and reach whatever it can reach. Never put keys in code, chats, documents or screenshots.

terms.one: Large clouds resell models inside their own accounts: Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Azure AI Foundry.
terms.why: Enterprises often must use their existing cloud for billing, security reviews, private networking and data residency.

terms.one: The prompt is everything you send: instructions, data, examples and the question. The system prompt is the builder's standing instructions for the whole conversation: role, rules and output format.
terms.why: Most quality gains on a POC come from clearer prompts, not from a different model.

terms.one: The software around a model that turns it into a working tool. It builds the prompt, keeps the conversation, offers tools, runs them when the model asks, and decides when to stop.
terms.like: The model is the engine. The harness is the rest of the car: steering, brakes, dashboard.
terms.why: Two products using the same model can behave very differently because of their harness. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and your own agent code are all harnesses.

terms.one: A way for the model to ask the harness to run something: search, read a file, call an API. The model only asks; your code decides whether to run it and sends back the result.
terms.why: This is how an LLM touches real systems, so it is where permissions and approvals matter most.

terms.one: A model working in a loop: plan, use a tool, look at the result, continue, until the task is done.
terms.why: Powerful but harder to predict and test. Use a simple fixed workflow when that is enough.

terms.one: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. A system is exposed once as an MCP server, and any app that supports MCP can use it.
terms.like: A USB-C port for AI tools: one plug shape that many devices understand.
terms.why: Lets a client connect their systems once and reuse them across AI tools, instead of building a custom integration for each.

terms.one: A harness for software work. It reads your repository, edits files, runs tests and commands. Examples: Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI), Gemini CLI (Google), Cursor and GitHub Copilot.
terms.why: The fastest way to build a POC, as long as you review every change and understand what it ran.

links.title: Codex: lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal
What is the Model Context Protocol?

groups.title: Context: what the model can see
groups.intro: A model knows only two things: what it learned in training, and what is in front of it right now. That second part is the context. Most quality problems in a POC are context problems: the right fact was missing, buried or drowned in noise.

diagrams.title: What goes into one request
diagrams.caption: The harness assembles all of this, in order, every single time. The model sees nothing else.

steps.label: System prompt
steps.note: Role, rules, output format

steps.label: Conversation so far
steps.note: Resent by the harness each time

steps.label: Retrieved documents
steps.note: Policy pages, past cases, records

steps.label: Tool results
steps.note: What a search or API call returned

steps.label: Your new message
steps.note: The actual question or task

steps.label: Model answers
steps.note: Using only training plus this context

terms.one: Everything the model can see for one request: the system prompt, conversation history, documents, tool results and your latest message.
terms.like: The papers on the desk of a very fast reader who remembers nothing from yesterday.
terms.why: If a fact is not in its training and not in the context, the model can only guess. Your job is to put the right facts on the desk.

terms.one: The maximum amount of text, in tokens, a model can take in one request, including its answer. Current large models handle hundreds of thousands of tokens, some up to a million.
terms.why: Large, but not free: every token costs money and time, and quality can drop when the key fact is buried in a huge pile.

terms.one: The model itself does not remember earlier requests. Chat apps seem to remember because the harness resends the conversation each time.
terms.why: In your own build, you must send the history, or a summary of it, yourself.

terms.one: A harness feature that saves notes between sessions, such as preferences or past decisions, and adds them back into the context later.
terms.why: It is the harness storing text, not the model learning. Know what is saved and where, because it may hold client data.

terms.one: The date after which the model saw no training data.
terms.why: It does not know about later events, prices or policy changes unless you put them in the context.

terms.one: First search your documents for the passages that matter, then put them into the context with the question, and ask the model to answer from them.
terms.why: The standard way to answer from client documents with citations, without retraining anything.

terms.one: Deciding what goes into the context, in what order and how much, so the model has what it needs and nothing that distracts it.
terms.why: More is not always better. Irrelevant text raises cost and can lower quality.

terms.one: Reusing the already-processed start of a prompt, such as a long policy document, across many requests so the repeated part is cheaper and faster.
terms.why: A simple cost and speed win when every request starts with the same large instructions or documents.

terms.one: The cap you set on how long an answer can be.
terms.why: Too low and answers get cut off mid-sentence; too high and a runaway answer costs more.

terms.one: The maximum requests or tokens your account may use per minute.
terms.why: Batch jobs over thousands of client documents hit these limits. Plan for retries and pacing.

links.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

groups.title: Open-weight and closed models
groups.intro: Some models you can download and run on your own machines. Others you can only use through the provider's service. Neither is always better; the choice depends on capability, data rules, cost and who will run it.

diagrams.title: Closed versus open-weight, side by side
diagrams.caption: Most client POCs start on a closed model through an API, then revisit the choice if data rules or cost demand it.

columns.title: Closed (API only)
items: Weights are never published
Use through the app, API or cloud partners
Usually the most capable models
Provider runs, scales and updates it
Data leaves your network, under contract terms

columns.title: Open-weight
items: Weights published for download
Run on your own cloud or servers
Strong, but often behind the frontier
You run, scale, patch and secure it
Data can stay fully inside your network

terms.one: A model whose weights are not published. You use it only through the provider's app or API, or a cloud partner. Examples: Claude, most GPT models, Gemini.
terms.why: Least effort to start and usually the most capable, but data goes to the provider under their terms.

terms.one: A model whose trained weights are published, so anyone can download and run it under its license. Examples: Llama (Meta), Gemma (Google), gpt-oss (OpenAI), and models from Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen.
terms.why: Can run entirely inside a client's network, but then you own hosting, scaling, updates and safety testing.

terms.one: Strictly, a model is open source only when the weights, the code and enough detail about the training data to rebuild it are available under a license that allows any use. Many models called open are open-weight only.
terms.why: Licenses differ and some restrict commercial use or large companies. Read the license; the client's legal team will ask.

terms.one: The most capable models available at a given time, usually from the large labs and usually closed.
terms.why: A sensible default for a POC, because it shows what is possible before you optimize for cost.

terms.one: Running a model on servers you control, in your own cloud account or data center.
terms.why: Useful when data must not leave, but it needs GPUs, engineering time and ongoing operations.

terms.one: A smaller model running on a laptop or a single server, using tools such as Ollama.
terms.why: Good for learning, offline demos and very sensitive tests. Usually less capable than frontier models.

terms.one: The legal terms for using a model's weights: commercial use, user limits and acceptable use rules.
terms.why: A model you cannot legally use in production is not an option, however good it is.

terms.one: A standard test used to compare models, such as a set of exam questions or coding tasks.
terms.why: Useful as a rough guide only. Your own evaluation on the client's real cases decides.

groups.title: Networks and cloud
groups.intro: Every AI solution moves data across networks: from a user's laptop, through the company network, over the internet, into a cloud and out to a model. You do not need to be a network engineer. You do need to know where the data travels and who can reach it, because that is the first thing a client's security team will ask.

diagrams.title: The path of one request
diagrams.caption: Each hop is a place where data can be protected, logged or blocked.

steps.label: User's laptop
steps.note: Browser or app

steps.label: Company network or VPN
steps.note: Firewall rules apply

steps.label: Internet over HTTPS
steps.note: Encrypted in transit with TLS

steps.label: Cloud region and VPC
steps.note: Your app in a private network

steps.label: Model API
steps.note: Public endpoint or private link

terms.one: Computers connected so they can send data to each other. Your office network, home Wi-Fi and the internet are all networks.
terms.why: Every integration question is really a network question: can system A reach system B?

terms.one: The global network of networks. Traffic crosses many organizations' equipment on its way.
terms.why: Anything sent over it unencrypted can be read along the path.

terms.one: The numeric address of a device on a network, such as 203.0.113.10.
terms.why: Firewalls and allow-lists use IP addresses to decide who may connect.

terms.one: The internet's phone book. It turns names like api.example.com into IP addresses.
terms.why: When something cannot connect, a DNS problem is one of the first things to rule out.

terms.one: A numbered door on a computer for one kind of service. HTTPS normally uses port 443.
terms.why: Corporate firewalls often block every port except a few, which can stop a tool from working.

terms.one: HTTP is the format browsers and APIs use for requests and responses. HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS so nobody on the path can read or change it.
terms.why: Client data must only travel over HTTPS. Plain HTTP is not acceptable.

terms.one: Rules that allow or block traffic by address, port or application.
terms.why: Your POC may need a firewall change to reach a model API or a client system. Those requests take time; ask early.

terms.one: A Virtual Private Network: an encrypted tunnel from your device into a private network, so you can reach internal systems as if you were in the office.
terms.why: You will often need the client's VPN to reach their test systems.

terms.one: Renting computing, storage and services from providers such as AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud instead of owning the hardware.
terms.why: Most client systems and most AI services now run in a cloud.

terms.one: A geographic location where a cloud runs its data centers, such as Frankfurt or Virginia.
terms.why: Data residency rules can require data to stay in a country or region, which limits which services you can use.

terms.one: Your own isolated private network inside a public cloud. You decide its addresses, what can reach the internet and what cannot.
terms.like: A locked, private office floor inside a shared tower block.
terms.why: Client data usually lives inside a VPC. Your POC may need to run in the same VPC, or connect to it securely, to reach that data.

terms.one: A slice of a VPC. Public subnets can reach the internet directly; private subnets cannot.
terms.why: Databases sit in private subnets on purpose. That is why your laptop cannot simply connect to them.

terms.one: A way to reach a cloud service, including some model services, without traffic going over the public internet.
terms.why: Often a security requirement for enterprise AI, and a reason clients prefer models through their own cloud.

terms.one: Systems running in the company's own data center instead of a cloud.
terms.why: Older core systems often live here. Reaching them from a cloud POC needs a secure connection.

terms.one: The delay between sending a request and getting the response.
terms.why: Distance, network hops and model size all add to it. Users notice anything over a few seconds.

groups.title: Data, privacy and security
groups.intro: Clients hand you their most sensitive material: customer records, contracts, employee files, prices. Handling it carelessly can end an engagement, break the law and hurt real people. Learn these words, because the client's security and legal teams use them in every conversation.
points: Trust: one leak or careless paste can end the engagement and the relationship.
Law: privacy laws such as the EU GDPR allow large fines, and they apply even to a test or a POC.
Contracts: client agreements often limit where data may go and who may see it.
AI tools: anything you paste into a tool may be stored or logged, and under some consumer plans used for training. Use only approved tools and accounts.
People: behind every record is a customer, patient or employee who never agreed to be in your demo.

diagrams.title: Can this data go to an AI service?
diagrams.caption: When in doubt, stop and ask the client's data owner. It is never your call alone.
diagrams.start: You want to send client data to a model
diagrams.question: What kind of data is it, and what is approved?

branches.result: Do not send it. Use synthetic or masked data until an approved setup exists.
Send only the fields the task needs, keep a log, follow the agreed retention.
Fine to use. Still keep keys, passwords and internal names out.

terms.one: Information that identifies a person directly or indirectly: name, email, phone number, ID numbers, and under many laws also location and online identifiers.
terms.why: Most privacy laws attach duties to personal data. Spot it before it goes anywhere.

terms.one: Data that needs extra protection: health, financial, biometric and children's data, among others defined by law. Commercially sensitive data such as prices, contracts and source code also counts for clients.
terms.why: Sensitive data usually needs explicit approval, stronger controls and sometimes cannot leave the client at all.

terms.one: The rules about personal data: what may be collected, for what purpose, who may see it and how long it is kept.
terms.why: The question it answers is: are we allowed to use this data in this way?
terms.vs: Privacy is about the rules for using data. Security is about protecting data. You can be perfectly secure and still break privacy rules, for example by using data for a purpose people never agreed to.

terms.one: Protecting data from unauthorized access, change or loss, through encryption, access control and monitoring.
terms.why: The question it answers is: can anyone who should not see this data get to it?

terms.one: The EU General Data Protection Regulation sets rules for personal data of people in the EU, including purpose limits, data minimization and individual rights. Many other places have similar laws, and some sectors have their own, such as HIPAA for health data in the US.
terms.why: Ask the client which laws apply before you touch any data.

terms.one: Use only the data the task actually needs, and remove or mask the rest.
terms.why: The simplest privacy control an FDE can apply, every day, without asking anyone.

terms.one: Ways to remove or replace identifiers. Anonymized data can no longer be linked to a person. Pseudonymized data replaces names with codes but can be linked back with a separate key.
terms.why: Under GDPR, pseudonymized data is still personal data. Do not call it anonymous.

terms.one: Where data is physically stored and processed.
terms.why: Some clients require data to stay in one country or region, which rules out some services and regions.

terms.one: How long data is kept, including copies in logs, backups and at the AI provider.
terms.why: Agree retention up front and delete POC data when the engagement ends.

terms.one: Whether a provider uses your inputs to improve its models. Business API and enterprise plans of the major providers generally do not by default; consumer apps may, depending on the plan and settings.
terms.why: Terms change. Check the current terms for the exact product and plan before any client data goes in.

terms.term: Encryption in transit and at rest
terms.one: In transit means protected while moving, through HTTPS and TLS. At rest means protected while stored on disk.
terms.why: Both are basic expectations in every security review.

terms.one: Give each person, service and AI tool only the access it needs, and nothing more.
terms.why: An assistant that only needs to read tickets must not be able to delete them or read payroll.

terms.one: Keeping API keys, passwords and tokens in a secret store or environment variables, never in code, documents or chats.
terms.why: Leaked keys are one of the most common and most avoidable incidents.

terms.one: A record of who did what and when, including what the AI suggested and what a person approved.
terms.why: Required in regulated work, and the first thing anyone asks for when something goes wrong.

terms.one: An attack where text inside a document, email or web page contains instructions meant to make the model do something else, such as reveal data or call a tool.
terms.why: Any content the model reads can try to steer it. Limit what tools and data it can reach, and keep a person in the loop for risky actions.

terms.one: The checks a client runs before approving a vendor: a data processing agreement (DPA), a security questionnaire and certifications such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001.
terms.why: These can take weeks. Start them as early as possible on an engagement.

groups.title: Building and shipping software
groups.intro: Words you will hear in every engineering conversation. If you come from a business background, these are enough to follow along on day one; module 3 goes deeper.

diagrams.title: The parts of a typical application
diagrams.caption: Read top to bottom: what users see, down to what everything runs on.

layers.label: Backend
layers.note: Logic, API calls, keys kept here

terms.one: The part of an application people see and click: a web page, a mobile screen.
terms.why: Never put secrets in the frontend. Anything sent to a browser can be read by its user.

terms.one: Server-side code that holds the logic, talks to databases and calls other APIs, including model APIs.
terms.why: This is where your model calls and API keys belong.

terms.one: Organized storage for records. Relational databases such as Postgres and SQL Server store data in tables you query with SQL.
terms.why: Most client data you need sits in a database you will query or receive an export from.

terms.one: A plain-text format for structured data, made of names and values, used by almost every API.
terms.why: You will ask models to return JSON so your code can use the result reliably.

terms.one: Git records every change to code. A repository is a project folder with its full history. GitHub and GitLab host repositories online.
terms.why: Every POC lives in a repository so others can review, run and continue it.

terms.one: A separate copy of a system: development for building, test for checking, production for real users.
terms.why: Never test on production systems or production data without explicit permission.

terms.one: Putting a version of software where its users can reach it.
terms.why: A POC is not finished until someone other than you can open it.

terms.one: A package of an application plus everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any machine.
terms.why: The usual way to hand a client something they can run inside their own cloud.

terms.one: Running code without managing servers. The platform runs it when needed and charges per use.
terms.why: A quick, cheap way to host a small POC.

terms.one: Automated pipelines that test every change (continuous integration) and release it (continuous delivery or deployment).
terms.why: Keeps quality steady as the POC changes quickly.

terms.one: A POC proves it can work on realistic data. A pilot proves it works for real users in real work. Production is the supported, monitored service.
terms.why: Be clear which one you are building. Each needs different quality, security and support.

terms.one: A set of test cases with expected results, used to measure how well an AI solution works.
terms.why: The difference between it seems to work and it works on 54 of 60 real cases.
